schleswig-holstein: Two old duchies in one hyphen: Schleswig is the Schlei inlet plus -wik, a trading bay, and Holstein is from Holseten, "dwellers in the woods".
Denmark ruled it, Prussia took it in 1864, and the border only settled by plebiscite in 1920 — which is why there are still Danish schools in the north.
mecklenburg-vorpommern: Mecklenburg is "the great castle" in Low German, and Pommern is Slavic po more, "by the sea" — Vor- means the near half, the far half being in Poland.
The emptiest state in Germany: more lakes than anywhere else, and fewer people per square kilometre than anywhere except the far north.
hamburg: From Hammaburg, a castle Charlemagne built around 825 — hamma is a bend in a river, and the Elbe bends here.
Officially the Free and Hanseatic City: the Hanse's habits of independence are still in its name and in its number plates, HH.
bremen: From bremo, Old Saxon for "edge" — the town sat on the bank of the Weser where the ground rose above the marsh.
The smallest state, and a strange shape: it is two cities, Bremen and Bremerhaven, 60 km apart with Niedersachsen in between.
niedersachsen: "Lower Saxony" — lower meaning downstream, towards the sea, not southern. The Saxons are the same people who gave Sachsen its name, but they started here.
So the two Saxonies are not neighbours: the name travelled south-east with a duke's title in the twelfth century, while the people stayed put.
berlin: Not the bear: it is most likely Slavic berl-, a swamp — the bear on the coat of arms is a pun that came later and stuck.
An island in Brandenburg, and its own state; the two have voted twice on merging and said no both times.
brandenburg: From Brennaburg, a Slavic stronghold the Germans took in 928 — the Havel marshes around it are why it was worth holding.
The core of Prussia: the Margrave of Brandenburg became the King in Prussia, and everything from there to Königsberg followed.
sachsen-anhalt: A 1945 invention joining Prussian Saxony to the old principality of Anhalt, whose name is simply a castle called Anhalt — "hold on".
Luther nailed his theses in Wittenberg here, and Bach was born in Eisenach just over the Thuringian border.
nordrhein-westfalen: The northern Rhineland plus Westfalen, "the western plain" — falen is an old word for flat open land, and there were Ostfalen to match.
The most populous state, by a distance: one German in five lives here, most of them in the Ruhr.
thuringen: Named for the Thuringii, a people Rome knew by the fourth century; nobody is sure where their own name came from.
Called the green heart of Germany, and it is the geographic centre of the country as well as the wooded one.
sachsen: The Saxons again — but they never lived here. The name came with the Ascanian dukes in 1423, six hundred kilometres from where the Saxons actually were.
Meissen porcelain was invented here in 1708, the first true porcelain made outside China.
hessen: From the Chatti, a tribe Tacitus wrote about; Chatti became Hessi became Hessen.
Its landgraves rented soldiers to Britain in the 1770s, which is why American schoolchildren learn the word Hessians.
rheinland-pfalz: The Rhineland plus the Pfalz, which is Latin palatium, a palace — the Count Palatine was the emperor's deputy, and his lands kept the title.
Two thirds of German wine comes from here, and the Mosel's vineyards are among the steepest anywhere.
saarland: Simply the land on the Saar, the river that runs through it.
It voted twice on its own future: in 1935 to rejoin Germany, and in 1955 against becoming independent — so it joined West Germany in 1957, the last piece to arrive.
bayern: From the Baiuvarii, "the men from Baia" — most likely Bohemia, which they left around the sixth century.
The oldest state in the list: a duchy from 555, a kingdom from 1806, and it joined the German Empire in 1871 keeping its own army and postal service.
baden-wurttemberg: Two names welded together in 1952: Baden is Old High German for baths, the Roman springs at Baden-Baden, and Württemberg is a castle hill whose own name nobody has explained.
The Black Forest is here, and so is the source of the Danube — which then runs 2,850 km east to the Black Sea.
